title: Jere D. Gallagher
text:
in memorium
Throughout her career, Dr. Jere Dee Gallagher was highly regarded and esteemed as an authority on child development. She dedicated most of her time to the University of Pittsburgh’s School of Education, where she eventually rose to the position of associate dean. During her tenure, she was instrumental in creating the Kinder Kinetics Program in the Health and Physical Activity Department, which she directed for over 25 years and considered her life’s crowning achievement

The FG-COMPASS web app walks you through the decision tree for each skill: answer one or two yes/no questions and get the child’s level from 1 to 4. It works on phones, tablets and laptops, so you can use it in the gym, in class or in the clinic.

All 10 skills, five locomotor and five object control, using the v2.2 decision trees.
Setup and instructions for each skill: what to set up, what to say to the child and notes for the rater.
Session results: a table of levels by child and skill, which you can download as a CSV file or print.
English for now. A Portuguese version will follow, using the validated Portuguese wording of the decision trees.

title: Web app
text:
Privacy
Nothing is saved online or in your browser. Results disappear when you close or reload the page, so download the CSV first if you need it. That makes the web app a good fit for teaching and practice: students can rate classmates or videos without creating accounts or storing children’s data.






This is a prototype for teaching and practice. For research data collection, follow the testing protocols and record forms on the Download page.



The earlier prototype (overhand throw only) is still online.

title: See how well a child moves, in two yes/no questions per skill.
text:
Movement skills assessment · Ages 5–10
      See how well a child moves, in two yes/no questions per skill.
      FG-COMPASS rates 10 everyday movement skills, like throwing, kicking and jumping, on a simple 1–4 scale. You watch the child live. No video, no long checklists.
      
        Download the decision trees
        See how it works 
      
      
        Free PDF
        Peer-reviewed reliability
        Works in a gym, clinic or lab

        Try it

      10movement skills
      2subtests: locomotor and object control
      5–10years of age
      4proficiency levels
      Liveobservation, no video needed
    
  




  
    
      Who it's for
      Practical enough for the gym, rigorous enough for the lab.
      Pick your role to see what FG-COMPASS gives you and where to start.
    
    
      
        PE teachers & coachesClasses and teams
        Clinicians & early childhoodTherapy and early years
        Researchers & studentsStudies and theses
        Parents & administratorsFamilies and programs
      
      
        Check a whole class in a regular lesson.
        Two quick questions per skill keep the pace of a normal class. Rate every child on the same 1–4 scale and see who needs help with what.
        
        
      
    
  




  
    
      How it works
      Watch, answer, score. That's it.
    
    
      1Watch the child perform a skillObserve live, in the gym, playground or clinic. A short protocol covers setup, instructions and trials for each skill.
      2Answer two yes/no questionsThe first question points toward the lower or upper levels. A second question confirms where the child lands.
      3Record a level from 1 to 4A level for each skill builds the child's profile, so you can track progress or compare before and after a program.
    

    
      
        One tree, four possible paths
        Every skill uses the same three-question tree. Each child follows one path: a key question, then one confirming question.
        
          Level 1
          Level 2
          Level 3
          Level 4
        
        
      
      
        
          No
          Yes
          Yes
          No
          No
          Yes
          QUESTION 1Key feature seen?
          QUESTION 2Early pattern confirmed?
          QUESTION 2Proficient pattern confirmed?
          Level 1INITIAL
          Level 2EMERGING
          Level 3DEVELOPING
          Level 4PROFICIENT
        
      
    

    
      For researchers: the composite decision-tree model
      
        FG-COMPASS is a process-oriented, criterion-referenced instrument. Each skill is scored with a composite decision tree that combines the Observational Plan (Haywood & Getchell, 2009) and Three-Stage (McClenaghan & Gallahue, 1978) approaches to FMS assessment, using only three key performance criteria drawn from validated and hypothesized developmental sequences (Furtado, 2009).
        
          Discriminatory question (DQ) separates the extremes (levels 1 and 4).
          Upper confirmatory question (UCQ) confirms level 4; if not confirmed, the child is level 3.
          Lower confirmatory question (LCQ) confirms level 1; if not confirmed, the child is level 2.
        
        
          References
          
            Furtado, O., Jr. (2009). Development and initial validation of the Furtado-Gallagher Computerized Observational Movement Pattern Assessment System (FG-COMPASS) [Doctoral dissertation, University of Pittsburgh]. d-scholarship.pitt.edu/8917
            Haywood, K. M., & Getchell, N. (2009). Life span motor development (5th ed.). Human Kinetics.
            McClenaghan, B. A., & Gallahue, D. L. (1978). Fundamental movement: Observation and assessment. W. B. Saunders.
          
        
      
    
  




  
    
      Reading the results
      What the four levels mean
      Example: the overhand throw, from the first attempts to a proficient throwing pattern.
    
    
      
        1InitialThe key proficient feature is missing and the early pattern is confirmed.In the throwThe trunk faces the target and there is no step forward.
      
        2EmergingThe key feature is still missing, but the child has moved past the early pattern.In the throwLittle or no trunk rotation, but the child steps forward.
      
        3DevelopingThe key feature is present, but the proficient pattern is not yet complete.In the throwThe trunk rotates, with a short step on the opposite foot.
      
        4ProficientThe key feature is present and the proficient pattern is confirmed.In the throwThe trunk rotates, with a long step on the opposite foot (at least half the child's height).
    
    
    First attemptsProficient pattern
  




  
    
      What it measures
      Ten skills, two subtests.
    
    
      
        LocomotorMoving the body from place to place.
        SkippingHoppingHorizontal jumpVertical jumpGalloping
      
      
        Object controlSending, receiving and controlling a ball.
        ThrowingCatchingKickingBattingStationary dribble
      
    
  




  
    
      The evidence
      Built on more than 15 years of research.
      Developed at the University of Pittsburgh and tested for reliability and agreement with expert raters in peer-reviewed studies.
      Why movement skills matterChildren who move well tend to be more active. Research links these skills to healthier body composition, working memory and more confident play with peers.
      See all publications

title: Ovande Furtado JR
text:
Dr. Furtado received a B.A. in Physical Education from the Federal University of Parana, Curitiba, PR - Brazil. He earned his M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in Motor Behavior from the University of Pittsburgh, PA. Dr. Furtado’s line of research focuses on two main areas: (1) validation of observational models in psychomotor assessment instruments and (2) the relationship between motor skill competence, perceived motor competence, physical activity levels, and body composition.
